items.question: Source A. Orla Bakeries runs a central bakery and 24 shops in Hong Kong. Extracts from its accounts, with last year in brackets: revenue $40m ($32m); cost of sales $24m ($17.6m); other operating expenses $10m ($9.4m); interest $0.8m ($0.2m); non-current assets $29m ($18.5m); current assets $6m ($4.5m), including inventory $2.5m ($1.5m); current liabilities $5m ($3m); non-current liabilities, all bank loans at 8% a year, $10m ($2.5m); total equity $20m ($17.5m). This year it built a new central bakery, financed mainly by a bank loan, and won a supermarket contract at lower prices than its shops charge. Its shops employed an average of 200 staff (180), of whom 60 (27) left during the year; replacing each leaver costs $8,000. Absence lost 2,500 of 50,000 possible working days (1,350 of 45,000). Its 50 bakers made 150,000 loaves a month (40 bakers, 128,000). Shop staff earn $2,000 a month; the two largest rival chains pay $2,200. Most leavers named pay as a reason, and many said shift rotas were changed at a day's notice without anyone asking them. The directors are considering an employee share ownership scheme costing about $500,000 a year, whose shares are lost by anyone who leaves within three years, and a second new bakery, also to be financed by a bank loan. Evaluate whether Orla Bakeries should finance its second new bakery with another bank loan. (20 marks)

items.question: Source A. Tanjong Bakes is a chain of 40 bakery-cafés in Singapore with 900 staff and a central bakery that supplies every café. Last year its sales were S$60m and its profit S$6m, and it held 8% of the country's bakery-café market. The central bakery makes 20,000 loaves a day at a cost of S$0.80 a loaf; new ovens would let it make 50,000 a day at S$0.62 a loaf. The directors are choosing between two ways to grow. Plan A is to open 15 cafés over two years, each costing S$400,000, paid for from retained profit. Plan B is to take over Golden Crust, a rival with 30 cafés and 6% of the market, for S$36m. Golden Crust's net assets are worth S$20m and it makes a profit of S$3m a year; combining the two chains is expected to save S$1.5m a year. Tanjong Bakes would borrow S$24m of the price at 6% a year. After the takeover the business would have 1,500 staff and 5 layers of management instead of 3. Tanjong Bakes has also agreed to sell frozen dough to supermarkets, which pay 60 days after delivery, while its flour supplier, Straits Flour Mill, must be paid within 30 days. The mill, which Tanjong Bakes pays S$4m a year, is for sale. Explain one disadvantage to Tanjong Bakes of growing organically through Plan A. (4 marks)

candidates.wording: Advantages and disadvantages of organic growth.

items.question: Source A. Serana is a Singaporean skincare brand sold in 6 countries. It runs one advertising campaign in all of them, which cost $1.2m; a separate campaign for each country would cost about $450,000. Its directors now plan to enter Zarand, a hot, dry country where most people are Muslim and speak their own language. In Zarand most skincare is bought in small family shops and online, and cheap local creams are popular. Spoken in Zarand's language, the name Serana sounds close to the word for "slippery". Serana also makes a halal-certified, alcohol-free serum for Muslim buyers. It estimates the number of likely buyers in five countries at 40,000, 25,000, 60,000, 15,000, 20,000. Each buyer uses 3 bottles a year at $30 a bottle, against $20 for a mass-market serum. Its current options include taking its existing moisturiser to Zarand, and launching a new hair-care range there. Assess whether Serana should compete in Zarand on low price or on being different.
